Under Law 12.2, an indirect free kick is awarded when a goalkeeper handles the ball inside their own penalty area after a teammate has deliberately kicked it to them. The free kick is taken from where the offence occurred, subject to the Law 13 rules on free kicks near the goal area. No disciplinary sanction applies because no goal-scoring opportunity was denied.

Under Law 12, a goalkeeper commits an offence by handling the ball inside their own penalty area after it has been deliberately kicked to them by a teammate. The sanction is an indirect free kick to the opposing team, taken from where the offence occurred (subject to Law 13 positioning). No disciplinary sanction is required because no goal-scoring opportunity was denied.

Under Law 12.2, an indirect free kick is awarded when a goalkeeper handles the ball inside their own penalty area after a teammate has deliberately kicked it to them. The kick is taken from where the offence occurred, subject to the Law 13 rules on free kicks taken near the goal area. Under Law 11, a player in an offside position who receives the ball from an opponent who deliberately played it (other than a deliberate save) is not considered to have gained an advantage, and a poor or misdirected deliberate play does not change this. The Blue defender was in control and deliberately played the ball, so the Red forward is not penalised and play continues.

Under Law 11, a player in an offside position who receives the ball from an opponent who deliberately played it (other than a deliberate save) is not considered to have gained an advantage. Under Law 13, once the ball is kicked and clearly moves it is in play, and the kicker must not touch it again before it has touched another player. A second touch by the kicker is an offence penalised by an indirect free kick to Blue from where it occurred (Law 13.4). No sanction applies unless the second touch is itself a handball or a separate disciplinary offence.

Under Law 13 (and Law 9/12 double-touch provisions), once the free kick is taken and the ball is in play, the kicker must not touch it again before it has touched another player. Doing so is an offence penalised by an indirect free kick to the opposing team (Blue) from where the second touch occurred. No disciplinary sanction is required unless another offence was committed.

Under Law 13, once the ball is kicked and clearly moves it is in play, and the kicker must not touch it again before it has touched another player. A second touch by the kicker (not a handball) is penalised with an indirect free kick to the opponents from the position of the second touch, with no disciplinary sanction.

Under Law 14, the penalty kicker must not play the ball again until it has touched another player. Rebounding off the post does not count. Blue is awarded an indirect free kick from where the second touch occurred (Laws 13/14), and no disciplinary sanction is required.

Under Law 14, once the penalty kick is taken the kicker must not play the ball again until it has touched another player. Rebounding off the goalpost does not count as another player's touch, so the second touch is a double-touch offence. Blue is awarded an indirect free kick from where the kicker touched the ball again; no card is required.

Under Law 14, the kicker must not touch the ball again until it has touched another player; a rebound off the goalpost does not count. Playing it a second time is a double-touch offence, so Blue is awarded an indirect free kick from the place of the second touch, with no disciplinary sanction.

The caution would be upgraded to a sending-off only if the interference denied an obvious goal-scoring opportunity, which is not indicated here.

Under Law 8, when play is stopped with no offence and the ball is inside the penalty area, the ball is dropped for the defending team's goalkeeper in their penalty area. It does not matter that a Red attacker touched it last, so the dropped ball goes to Blue's goalkeeper.

Under Law 8, when play is stopped with no offence and the ball is in the penalty area, the ball is dropped for the defending team's goalkeeper in their penalty area, regardless of who last touched it. Since the ball was in Blue's penalty area, it is dropped for Blue's goalkeeper.

Under Law 12, a goalkeeper who controls the ball with the hands for more than eight seconds is penalised with a corner kick to the opposing team, after the referee's visible five-second countdown. No disciplinary sanction applies to this offence alone.

Under Law 13, a goal cannot be scored directly into the kicker's own goal from a free kick; if the ball enters the kicker's own goal directly, a corner kick is awarded to the opposing team. Blue restarts with a corner kick.

Under Law 12, when a defender commits a DOGSO offence inside their own penalty area and a penalty kick is awarded, the sanction is reduced to a caution (yellow card) if the offence was an attempt to play the ball. Under Law 15 (2026/27), if the referee judges a throw-in is being deliberately delayed, they start a visible five-second countdown. If the throw-in is not taken before the countdown ends, the throw-in is awarded to the opposing team, so Blue takes the throw-in from the same place.

Under the 2026/27 Law 16 amendment, if the referee considers a goal kick is being delayed, they start a visual five-second countdown. If the kick is not taken before it ends, a corner kick is awarded to the opponents, here Red. No caution is needed for the delay itself, as the change of restart is the sanction.

Under Law 14, when a penalty kicker slips and the ball accidentally touches their other foot or leg, the kick is retaken if it goes in. This replaces the usual indirect free kick for a double touch. The touch was accidental, so no sanction is given.
